output.text_basic:
.

Here's a list of what seems to be an endless parade of sleeping bags from a recent camping trip. They are all exactly the same – thick, beige, and boring.

Your brain can think of many ways to improve their sleeping bags: new designs, features, accessories, variations on existing features, ways to make the bag more useful for different purposes, and improvements to the material, color, shape, packing method, size, price, and so on.

For example, your Creative Thinking session might generate these ideas:

  • A sleeping bag with solar panel strips so you can charge your phone while you sleep.
  • A sleeping bag with built-in pillow compartment.
  • A sleeping bag with a soft shell and a removable lining so you can adapt to the temperature.
  • A detachable sleeping bag cover for year-round use.
  • A fold-out pocket on the sleeping bag for storing small items.
  • A smaller, lighter sleeping bag for kids.
  • A sleeping bag with a waterproof layer for those rainy night camp-outs.

So let's imagine that you've come up with 20 creative ideas to improve the sleeping bag. But now what?

Turning Creative Thoughts into Practical Ideas

Generating creative ideas is the first step to finding breakthrough innovations, but transforming those ideas into practical and implementable concepts is just as important. Otherwise, your creative efforts become lost in the noise, and never result in actual progress.

The practicality assessment phase of the Creative Problem Solving Process involves two key steps:

  • Assessing the Value of the Idea
  • Assessing the Feasibility of the Idea

Assessing the Value of an Idea

Think about the impact your idea will have on the intended target market or users of your product. Is the new feature important to them? Will it solve a significant problem or improve their lives in some way? Is it something they want or need enough to pay for?

You can answer these questions with market research, customer feedback or by using your own knowledge and experience. But however you gather this information, it's important to assess the value your potential new feature holds.

Assessing the Feasibility of an Idea

Feasibility encompasses the many factors involved in the actual implementation of a product improvement idea.

Here are some aspects of feasibility to take into account:

  • Technical Feasibility – Is the technology or materials available to implement your idea? Or does it require the development of something new? How much time and money would it take to achieve this?
  • Economic Feasibility – Is it financially viable to produce your new product? Will the potential increased revenue exceed the production costs?
  • Schedule Feasibility – Can your idea be implemented within your required timeframe? How long will the development and production process take?
  • Market Feasibility – Is there a large enough customer base to make the new product a worthwhile investment? Will enough people be willing to buy it?
  • Marketing Feasibility – How will you communicate the benefits of the new feature to potential customers? What messages and channels will be most effective? How will you differentiate your product from competitors offering similar features?

For most practical and implementable ideas, the benefits should clearly outweigh the challenges in these areas. If not, then it might be useful to revise the idea or generate a new one.

Developing an Action Plan

Once you've identified those creative ideas that have high value potential and are feasible to implement, the next step is to develop a plan to bring them to life.

This will involve steps such as:

  • Gathering detailed information about the idea – Will you need more research, data, or feedback? Who will gather or analyze this information?
  • Developing preliminary designs, prototypes, or mock-ups.
  • Creating detailed cost estimates.
  • Planning a product development timeline.
  • Developing a go-to-market strategy.
  • Creating a test marketing or beta program.

It's also crucial at this point to regularly reassess progress and results, and be prepared to make adjustments as necessary. Iterative development and feedback loops will make your new feature far more successful.

Bringing Creativity and Practicality Together

It's a common misconception that creativity and practicality are opposing forces. In reality, the two need to work in tandem to turn innovative ideas into successful business outcomes.

The creative thinking process helps you come up with imaginative ideas, but it's the practicality assessment phase that ensures those ideas have potential value and can be practically implemented.

So whether you're improving a sleeping bag, a new software feature, a service offering, or any other type of product or concept, make sure you balance your creative thinking skills with a well-thought-out plan for bringing those ideas to life.

How to Stimulate Your Creative Mind

Creative thinkers have trained their brains to be constantly receptive to stimulus from the external environment - and they've learned how to use this stimulus as fodder for their creative work.

The main difference between creative thinkers and others is their ability to notice things - the small, seemingly insignificant things that most people overlook.

Start With Something Small

Question: Creativity Improvement Task. You'll be presented with a object, and your task is to suggest as many ways as you can think of to improve the object. Here's the object: Sleeping Bag
Answer: .

Here's a list of what seems to be an endless parade of sleeping bags from a recent camping trip. They are all exactly the same – thick, beige, and boring.

Your brain can think of many ways to improve their sleeping bags: new designs, features, accessories, variations on existing features, ways to make the bag more useful for different purposes, and improvements to the material, color, shape, packing method, size, price, and so on.

For example, your Creative Thinking session might generate these ideas:

  • A sleeping bag with solar panel strips so you can charge your phone while you sleep.
  • A sleeping bag with built-in pillow compartment.
  • A sleeping bag with a soft shell and a removable lining so you can adapt to the temperature.
  • A detachable sleeping bag cover for year-round use.
  • A fold-out pocket on the sleeping bag for storing small items.
  • A smaller, lighter sleeping bag for kids.
  • A sleeping bag with a waterproof layer for those rainy night camp-outs.

So let's imagine that you've come up with 20 creative ideas to improve the sleeping bag. But now what?

Turning Creative Thoughts into Practical Ideas

Generating creative ideas is the first step to finding breakthrough innovations, but transforming those ideas into practical and implementable concepts is just as important. Otherwise, your creative efforts become lost in the noise, and never result in actual progress.

The practicality assessment phase of the Creative Problem Solving Process involves two key steps:

  • Assessing the Value of the Idea
  • Assessing the Feasibility of the Idea

Assessing the Value of an Idea

Think about the impact your idea will have on the intended target market or users of your product. Is the new feature important to them? Will it solve a significant problem or improve their lives in some way? Is it something they want or need enough to pay for?

You can answer these questions with market research, customer feedback or by using your own knowledge and experience. But however you gather this information, it's important to assess the value your potential new feature holds.

Assessing the Feasibility of an Idea

Feasibility encompasses the many factors involved in the actual implementation of a product improvement idea.

Here are some aspects of feasibility to take into account:

  • Technical Feasibility – Is the technology or materials available to implement your idea? Or does it require the development of something new? How much time and money would it take to achieve this?
  • Economic Feasibility – Is it financially viable to produce your new product? Will the potential increased revenue exceed the production costs?
  • Schedule Feasibility – Can your idea be implemented within your required timeframe? How long will the development and production process take?
  • Market Feasibility – Is there a large enough customer base to make the new product a worthwhile investment? Will enough people be willing to buy it?
  • Marketing Feasibility – How will you communicate the benefits of the new feature to potential customers? What messages and channels will be most effective? How will you differentiate your product from competitors offering similar features?

For most practical and implementable ideas, the benefits should clearly outweigh the challenges in these areas. If not, then it might be useful to revise the idea or generate a new one.

Developing an Action Plan

Once you've identified those creative ideas that have high value potential and are feasible to implement, the next step is to develop a plan to bring them to life.

This will involve steps such as:

  • Gathering detailed information about the idea – Will you need more research, data, or feedback? Who will gather or analyze this information?
  • Developing preliminary designs, prototypes, or mock-ups.
  • Creating detailed cost estimates.
  • Planning a product development timeline.
  • Developing a go-to-market strategy.
  • Creating a test marketing or beta program.

It's also crucial at this point to regularly reassess progress and results, and be prepared to make adjustments as necessary. Iterative development and feedback loops will make your new feature far more successful.

Bringing Creativity and Practicality Together

It's a common misconception that creativity and practicality are opposing forces. In reality, the two need to work in tandem to turn innovative ideas into successful business outcomes.

The creative thinking process helps you come up with imaginative ideas, but it's the practicality assessment phase that ensures those ideas have potential value and can be practically implemented.

So whether you're improving a sleeping bag, a new software feature, a service offering, or any other type of product or concept, make sure you balance your creative thinking skills with a well-thought-out plan for bringing those ideas to life.

. Write down five ways you could make a car key better.

Got them? Good.

Now, consider this: How many of your five ideas were actually practical? How many were simply outlandish or extreme?

More importantly, how do your practical and impractical ideas compare? If you're like most people, then you probably came up with a laundry list of impractical ideas first, followed by a short list of practical ones. Here's the thing:

Most people consider creativity to be all about the zany and the extreme - the "crazy" ideas. (And this isn't necessarily helped by the way creativity is often depicted in cartoons and movies, where characters come up with one outrageous idea after another.) But being extremely creative isn't necessarily about how outside-the-box your ideas are.

Rather, it's about finding truly unique solutions that work.

This is where divergent thinking - generating lots of possible answers - meets convergent thinking - deciding which answers are the best.

So the next time you're presented with a creative challenge, try following these steps:

1. Brainstorm for a set period of time (the more ideas, the better).
2. Eliminate impractical ideas.
3. Rank the remainder by their potential impact and feasibility.

Brainstorming Techniques for Improving Objects

Start your thinking with the object as is and build upon it. Here are some brainstorming techniques which may help you come up with creative ideas:
1.  Morphological Analysis. Break the object down into its characteristics. Look at each feature and systematically change them one at a time. For example, with a watering can, you might explore features such as the handle, the nozzle, the container, the fill hole, etc.

2.  Dissect and Reassemble. Mentally "dissect" the object and rearrange it in different ways. For example, instead of having a container at the top of a watering can, imagine the container at the bottom or even having a reservoir surrounding the handle.

3.  Divide and Conquer. Break the object into parts and look at alternative parts to use. For example, what else could you use for a watering can handle? Rope, a stick, a bicycle frame? What about the container? Could you use an old garden hose, a bladder, a woven basket?

**Problem Statement:** How can we improve a hair tie?

1. **Material Friction:** The material is too slippery, leading to the tie sliding off easily.
2. **Weakness:** The tie breaks easily under pressure, causing inconvenience.
3. **Visibility:** The tie is too small or blends in with hair, making it hard to see and remove.
4. **Uncomfortable:** The tie is not made of materials that are gentle on the hair, causing discomfort and potential hair loss.

1. **Improved Material:** Utilize anti-slippery materials that enhance grip and reduce sliding.
2. **Durability:** Design the hair tie with stronger, more resilient materials that resist breaking.
3. **Increased Size/Visibility:** Make the ties larger or use contrasting colors/patterns to enhance visibility.
4. **Comfort-Friendly:** Use hypoallergenic, soft materials that won't tear hair or cause discomfort.

Of course, some of these ideas might suck. For instance, having transparency could result in people's privacy being compromised whenever they pay for something. Having objects poking out like hooks could tear holes in pockets. And carrying around solar panels adds considerable bulk and weight to the wallet.

However, many of these ideas could work. As a creative thinker, you need to brainstorm without judgment and then sift through the results, tossing out the bad ideas and fine-tuning the good ones.

Remember, it's impossible to think of perfect ideas off the bat. The best ideas require time and effort to refine. As a creative thinker, your raw output of ideas is just the starting point.

Now that you know the basics of improving creativity, let's explore some techniques that can help you enhance your skills:

  1. Challenge yourself.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about.
  3. Create a conducive environment for creativity.
  4. Learn to look at things from different perspectives.
  5. Foster curiosity.
  6. Improve your cognitive flexibility.
  7. Practice divergent thinking.
  8. Utilize metaphors strategically.
  9. Generate a lot of ideas and sort through them later.

Let's delve deeper into these techniques next.

Challenge Yourself

Challenging yourself is a powerful way to increase your capacity for creative thinking. Deliberately make things difficult for yourself to force your brain to adapt and grow. Here are some ways to do this:

  • Deliberately break your routines and do things differently.
  • Start a project that you're not sure you can complete.
  • Set higher goals and standards for yourself.

Engage With Things You're Passionate About

When you're passionate about something, you naturally engage more deeply. The more you engage, the more you know, and the more ideas you have to draw upon. Follow your interests and passions and let them drive your creativity.

Create a Conducive Environment for Creativity

Your environment can profoundly impact your creativity. To foster a creative environment, make sure:

  • You have sufficient resources.
  • You're comfortable physically.
  • You're in a safe and welcoming space.
  • You're free from distractions.
  • You have access to the tools you need.

Learn to Look at Things from Different Perspectives

When you can see the world or a problem from multiple perspectives, you can generate more ideas. Practice the following to learn how to do this:

  • Put yourself in someone else's shoes.
  • Get in touch with your emotions.
  • Question your assumptions.
  • Use empathy to understand another person's viewpoint.

Foster Curiosity

Curiosity leads to exploration, and exploration results in a wealth of ideas. Ask "why" and "what if" questions instead of settling for easy answers. Embrace your natural curiosity, and constantly seek to understand more about the world.

Improve Your Cognitive Flexibility

Cognitive flexibility refers to your ability to shift between ideas, perspectives, or operations. This allows you to be adaptable and creative in response to problems. Improve your cognitive flexibility by:

  • Practicing mindfulness and meditation.
  • Engaging in critical thinking.
  • Learning new skills.
  • Solving complex problems regularly.

Practice Divergent Thinking

Divergent thinking involves brainstorming many ideas without judgment. It's the opposite of convergent thinking, which entails analyzing a problem to arrive at a single answer or solution. To practice divergent thinking:

  • Use creativity exercises like the Creativity Improvement Task.
  • Engage in free association.
  • Employ techniques such as the mind-mapping method.

Utilize Metaphors Strategically

Metaphors can help you generate new ideas by bridging gaps between seemingly unrelated things. Use metaphors to inspire creative thinking, but be mindful of their limitations.

Generate a Lot of Ideas and Sort Through Them Later

This strategy is related to divergent thinking. When you're tackling a problem, don't worry about creating perfect solutions right off the bat. Instead, create as many ideas as possible and evaluate them later.

By incorporating these techniques into your daily life, you'll stimulate your creativity and improve your problem-solving abilities.

Let's look at some creative thinking examples to illustrate these concepts in practice.


Example 1: Innovative Office Design

Suppose you're an interior designer tasked with creating a more creative and productive office environment. You want to challenge yourself, engage with things you're passionate about, and create a conducive environment for creativity.

Considering these guidelines, you make the following decisions:

  • Challenge yourself by adopting a zero-based design approach, where you ignore existing office furniture conventions and start with a blank slate.
  • Engage with things you're passionate about by incorporating art and nature elements throughout the office, such as large windows for natural light, green spaces for relaxation, and whiteboards for sketching.
  • Create a conducive environment for creativity by providing comfortable seating options, collaborative spaces, and quiet areas for reflection.

By integrating these elements, you create an office that facilitates both productivity and creativity.

Example 2: Using Metaphors to Drive Innovation

Imagine you're a product developer tasked with improving the user experience of a tablet. You decide to utilize metaphors to inspire creative thinking.

You think about how different objects and environments work and how their functions might inspire new features for your tablet. Here are some ideas generated from this process:

  1. A chef's knife: A sharp, precise blade suggests creating more accurate stylus features or adding multi-touch functionality.
  2. A Swiss Army knife: Having many tools in one suggests adding more integrated, useful app features.
  3. A piano: The harmonic tones suggest enhancing audio capabilities.
  4. A rainforest: A lush, interconnected ecosystem suggests creating applications that interact and enhance one another.

By employing metaphors, you generate new ideas that could lead to improved tablet functionality.

Example 3: Improving a Process – The Case of a Restaurant

You're an operational consultant tasked with improving a popular restaurant chain. They want to enhance both their service and the dining experience. You decide to challenge yourself and engage with things you're passionate about.

Taking these principles into account, you propose the following:

  1. Challenge yourself: You conduct a root-cause analysis to uncover inefficiencies in the current service model. This might involve shadowing servers, observing their movements, and quantifying their workload.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about: You introduce a concept called "culinary storytelling" into the menu, which involves describing the origin of ingredients and the chef's inspiration for each dish, thus making the dining experience more rich and memorable.

By utilizing these strategies, you suggest real improvements that cater to both operational efficiency and the customer's dining experience—a double win.

Now that you've learned about creative thinking and seen some practical examples, let’s discuss why this skill is important.

Why Is Creative Thinking Important?

Creative thinking is vital in today's knowledge-driven society, where fast-paced change is the norm. Here's why you should consider honing your creative thinking skills:

  • Creative thinking fosters innovation. It allows individuals and organizations to constantly evolve and adapt to new challenges and opportunities.
  • It improves problem-solving abilities. Creative approaches to problem-solving can result in more sustainable outcomes as the solutions address root causes, rather than merely their symptoms.
  • It enhances teamwork. A creative team works more harmoniously, as individuals are more likely to share new ideas and collaborate on innovative solutions when encouraged to think outside the box.
  • It drives growth. Businesses need innovative products and services to succeed in a competitive market. Creative thinking leads to the creation of these new offerings.
  • It improves personal and professional satisfaction. Engaging in creative thinking is a mentally fulfilling process that boosts self-esteem and job satisfaction.

Ultimately, creativity can be a powerful asset in every field and situation. If you're a leader or an employee, if you're pursuing higher education or a fulfilling hobby, enhancing your creative skills can significantly impact your career and personal life.

Now that you understand the power of creative thinking, let's wrap this up and apply what you've learned.

Apply What You've Learned: Your Personal Challenge

Think about a recurring problem in your personal or professional life. Use your creative thinking skills to devise unconventional solutions. Remember to consider the various techniques we've discussed: challenging yourself, engaging with sources of passion, and fostering a creative environment.

Here's an example scenario:

Suppose your recurring problem—whether personal or professional—is that you're constantly running behind schedule.

Apply creative thinking to come up with innovative solutions:

  1. Challenge yourself: Deliberately sabotage your current schedule to force yourself into new habits.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about: Add something you love to your schedule to make it more enjoyable (for example, a daily meditation session).
  3. Create a conducive environment for creativity: Organize your workspace and schedule so that you can focus on important tasks without distractions.

By applying creative thinking, you can generate novel solutions to your recurring problem.

Key Points

Creative thinking is the ability to generate innovative ideas by considering various perspectives, questioning assumptions, and using unconventional approaches. Here are some key points in this lesson:

  1. Creativity is not just about being artistic. It involves coming up with novel ideas and practical solutions.
  2. You can improve your creativity by challenging yourself, engaging with things you're passionate about, and creating a suitable environment for creative thinking.
  3. Techniques to boost creativity include:
    1. Learning to look at things from different perspectives.
    2. Fostering curiosity.
    3. Enhancing cognitive flexibility.
    4. Practicing divergent thinking.
    5. Utilizing metaphors strategically.
  4. Generate a lot of ideas and refine them later on.
  5. Creative thinking is important because it fosters innovation, improves problem-solving abilities, enhances teamwork, drives growth, and improves personal and professional satisfaction.

Developing your creative thinking skills will allow you to approach problems more effectively, and it will boost your overall performance in various areas of your life.

Okay. What are some ways to make a wallet better? Here are a few possibilities:

  1. Make it smell good.
  2. Include a USB drive for saving important documents and photos.
  3. Make it out of paper so that you can draw on it.
  4. Have an RFID tag protector to prevent identity theft.
  5. Build in a portable phone charger.
  6. Put in padding so that the items inside don't get smashed.
  7. Add solar panels on the outside to recharge a device like a cell phone.
  8. Include a compartment for coins.
  9. Have a strap to attach it to your belt.
  10. The strap could also function as a measuring tape.
  11. Create transparency so you can see how much cash or cards you have.
  12. Make it heat-resistant so you can sit on it if you need to.
  13. Construct a pen that's hidden within the wallet.
  14. Make a wallet out of antibacterial material to keep it clean.
  15. Add small hooks that you could use to keep things together.

Of course, some of these ideas might suck. For instance, having transparency could result in people's privacy being compromised whenever they pay for something. Having objects poking out like hooks could tear holes in pockets. And carrying around solar panels adds considerable bulk and weight to the wallet.

However, many of these ideas could work. As a creative thinker, you need to brainstorm without judgment and then sift through the results, tossing out the bad ideas and fine-tuning the good ones.

Remember, it's impossible to think of perfect ideas off the bat. The best ideas require time and effort to refine. As a creative thinker, your raw output of ideas is just the starting point.

Now that you know the basics of improving creativity, let's explore some techniques that can help you enhance your skills:

  1. Challenge yourself.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about.
  3. Create a conducive environment for creativity.
  4. Learn to look at things from different perspectives.
  5. Foster curiosity.
  6. Improve your cognitive flexibility.
  7. Practice divergent thinking.
  8. Utilize metaphors strategically.
  9. Generate a lot of ideas and sort through them later.

Let's delve deeper into these techniques next.

Challenge Yourself

Challenging yourself is a powerful way to increase your capacity for creative thinking. Deliberately make things difficult for yourself to force your brain to adapt and grow. Here are some ways to do this:

  • Deliberately break your routines and do things differently.
  • Start a project that you're not sure you can complete.
  • Set higher goals and standards for yourself.

Engage With Things You're Passionate About

When you're passionate about something, you naturally engage more deeply. The more you engage, the more you know, and the more ideas you have to draw upon. Follow your interests and passions and let them drive your creativity.

Create a Conducive Environment for Creativity

Your environment can profoundly impact your creativity. To foster a creative environment, make sure:

  • You have sufficient resources.
  • You're comfortable physically.
  • You're in a safe and welcoming space.
  • You're free from distractions.
  • You have access to the tools you need.

Learn to Look at Things from Different Perspectives

When you can see the world or a problem from multiple perspectives, you can generate more ideas. Practice the following to learn how to do this:

  • Put yourself in someone else's shoes.
  • Get in touch with your emotions.
  • Question your assumptions.
  • Use empathy to understand another person's viewpoint.

Foster Curiosity

Curiosity leads to exploration, and exploration results in a wealth of ideas. Ask "why" and "what if" questions instead of settling for easy answers. Embrace your natural curiosity, and constantly seek to understand more about the world.

Improve Your Cognitive Flexibility

Cognitive flexibility refers to your ability to shift between ideas, perspectives, or operations. This allows you to be adaptable and creative in response to problems. Improve your cognitive flexibility by:

  • Practicing mindfulness and meditation.
  • Engaging in critical thinking.
  • Learning new skills.
  • Solving complex problems regularly.

Practice Divergent Thinking

Divergent thinking involves brainstorming many ideas without judgment. It's the opposite of convergent thinking, which entails analyzing a problem to arrive at a single answer or solution. To practice divergent thinking:

  • Use creativity exercises like the Creativity Improvement Task.
  • Engage in free association.
  • Employ techniques such as the mind-mapping method.

Utilize Metaphors Strategically

Metaphors can help you generate new ideas by bridging gaps between seemingly unrelated things. Use metaphors to inspire creative thinking, but be mindful of their limitations.

Generate a Lot of Ideas and Sort Through Them Later

This strategy is related to divergent thinking. When you're tackling a problem, don't worry about creating perfect solutions right off the bat. Instead, create as many ideas as possible and evaluate them later.

By incorporating these techniques into your daily life, you'll stimulate your creativity and improve your problem-solving abilities.

Example 1: Innovative Office Design

Suppose you're an interior designer tasked with creating a more creative and productive office environment. You want to challenge yourself, engage with things you're passionate about, and create a conducive environment for creativity.

Considering these guidelines, you make the following decisions:

  • Challenge yourself by adopting a zero-based design approach, where you ignore existing office furniture conventions and start with a blank slate.
  • Engage with things you're passionate about by incorporating art and nature elements throughout the office, such as large windows for natural light, green spaces for relaxation, and whiteboards for sketching.
  • Create a conducive environment for creativity by providing comfortable seating options, collaborative spaces, and quiet areas for reflection.

By integrating these elements, you create an office that facilitates both productivity and creativity.

Example 2: Using Metaphors to Drive Innovation

Imagine you're a product developer tasked with improving the user experience of a tablet. You decide to utilize metaphors to inspire creative thinking.

You think about how different objects and environments work and how their functions might inspire new features for your tablet. Here are some ideas generated from this process:

  1. A chef's knife: A sharp, precise blade suggests creating more accurate stylus features or adding multi-touch functionality.
  2. A Swiss Army knife: Having many tools in one suggests adding more integrated, useful app features.
  3. A piano: The harmonic tones suggest enhancing audio capabilities.
  4. A rainforest: A lush, interconnected ecosystem suggests creating applications that interact and enhance one another.

By employing metaphors, you generate new ideas that could lead to improved tablet functionality.

Example 3: Improving a Process – The Case of a Restaurant

You're an operational consultant tasked with improving a popular restaurant chain. They want to enhance both their service and the dining experience. You decide to challenge yourself and engage with things you're passionate about.

Taking these principles into account, you propose the following:

  1. Challenge yourself: You conduct a root-cause analysis to uncover inefficiencies in the current service model. This might involve shadowing servers, observing their movements, and quantifying their workload.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about: You introduce a concept called "culinary storytelling" into the menu, which involves describing the origin of ingredients and the chef's inspiration for each dish, thus making the dining experience more rich and memorable.

By utilizing these strategies, you suggest real improvements that cater to both operational efficiency and the customer's dining experience—a double win.

Now that you've learned about creative thinking and seen some practical examples, let’s discuss why this skill is important.

Why Is Creative Thinking Important?

Creative thinking is vital in today's knowledge-driven society, where fast-paced change is the norm. Here's why you should consider honing your creative thinking skills:

  • Creative thinking fosters innovation. It allows individuals and organizations to constantly evolve and adapt to new challenges and opportunities.
  • It improves problem-solving abilities. Creative approaches to problem-solving can result in more sustainable outcomes as the solutions address root causes, rather than merely their symptoms.
  • It enhances teamwork. A creative team works more harmoniously, as individuals are more likely to share new ideas and collaborate on innovative solutions when encouraged to think outside the box.
  • It drives growth. Businesses need innovative products and services to succeed in a competitive market. Creative thinking leads to the creation of these new offerings.
  • It improves personal and professional satisfaction. Engaging in creative thinking is a mentally fulfilling process that boosts self-esteem and job satisfaction.

Ultimately, creativity can be a powerful asset in every field and situation. If you're a leader or an employee, if you're pursuing higher education or a fulfilling hobby, enhancing your creative skills can significantly impact your career and personal life.

Now that you understand the power of creative thinking, let's wrap this up and apply what you've learned.

Apply What You've Learned: Your Personal Challenge

Think about a recurring problem in your personal or professional life. Use your creative thinking skills to devise unconventional solutions. Remember to consider the various techniques we've discussed: challenging yourself, engaging with sources of passion, and fostering a creative environment.

Suppose your recurring problem—whether personal or professional—is that you're constantly running behind schedule.

Apply creative thinking to come up with innovative solutions:

  1. Challenge yourself: Deliberately sabotage your current schedule to force yourself into new habits.
  2. Engage with things you're passionate about: Add something you love to your schedule to make it more enjoyable (for example, a daily meditation session).
  3. Create a conducive environment for creativity: Organize your workspace and schedule so that you can focus on important tasks without distractions.

By applying creative thinking, you can generate novel solutions to your recurring problem.

  2. You can improve your creativity by challenging yourself, engaging with things you're passionate about, and creating a suitable environment for creative thinking.

    1. Learning to look at things from different perspectives.
    2. Fostering curiosity.
    3. Enhancing cognitive flexibility.
    4. Practicing divergent thinking.
    5. Utilizing metaphors strategically.
  4. Generate a lot of ideas and refine them later on.
  5. Creative thinking is important because it fosters innovation, improves problem-solving abilities, enhances teamwork, drives growth, and improves personal and professional satisfaction.

Developing your creative thinking skills will allow you to approach problems more effectively, and it will boost your overall performance in various areas of your life.

output.text_cot:
.

First, let's consider what the common uses and problems are with spatulas. We know they are used for flipping food, stirring food, mixing batter in mixing bowls, scraping the sides of bowls, and spreading butter on bread, among other things. We also know some drawbacks. They can have odd angles when flipping resulting in missed flips, they can be too stiff to easily mix thin batters, they can be too narrow to effectively scrape the side of a bowl, and they can leave butter unevenly spread on bread.

When contemplating these issues, we can brainstorm potential improvements.

* Change the angle of the spatula head or the position of the handle - This would hopefully allow for more precise flipping, without as many near misses.

* Add a second adjustable head - This could provide a flatter side for mixing and scraping, as opposed to the more traditional rounded head, allowing for better mixing on bowls and efficient scraping. This could even have one side coarse and another side fine for different mixing scenarios.

* Make part of the spatula flexible - Perhaps the neck of the spatula, or even part of the head, could be of a flexible silicone, making it easier to scrape bowls clean and better for stirring thin batters. It could be heat-resistant, to maintain functionality with hot cooking.

* Add an ergonomic handle - A handle that fits comfortably in your hand and reduces stress on your hand and wrist could make preparing food easier and less painful.

* Create interchangeable heads - Having various heads that could quickly be swapped out could allow one spatula to be used for a variety of cooking tasks.

* A spatula with a cutting edge - This could provide a knife-like element to the spatula, allowing for cutting of food as well as stirring, flipping, and scraping.

It's important to consider your target user. Who is this improved spatula for? Consider different user needs. For example, someone with arthritis may prefer a more ergonomic handle and a head made of flexible silicone, while a professional chef may prefer the multi-functional aspect and the ability to quickly change the head for different cooking needs.

As you brainstorm, don't worry about making every idea perfect. Brainstorming is about quantity first, then quality. Once you have a good list of potential improvements, you can evaluate each one and see how feasible it might be, considering factors like materials, manufacturing, cost, user acceptance, and other important elements.

Creativity Improvement Task. Let's do another one.

Object: Toothbrush.

Common uses: Cleaning teeth, scrubbing small spots or dirt off of surfaces or items.

Potential problems: Brushes can wear out or fall apart, bristles can become misshapen and don't effectively clean teeth, not good for cleaning larger areas or tight spots.

Ideas for improvement:

* A toothbrush with replaceable heads - Just like electric toothbrushes, the brush itself can stay consistent, but the 'brush' part can be swapped out when it wears down, saving the handle and reducing waste.

* Increase bristle flexibility - The bristles could be made of a flexible material, like silicone, to keep them flexible and effective at cleaning despite pressure applied.

* Bristles that can adapt to your teeth - There could be an aspect to the toothbrush that allows for the adaptation of the bristle shape to match your teeth, offering maximum cleaning potential.

* Toothbrush with a scraper on the other end - This could be used to scrape plaque and food remnants off teeth and may also serve as a tongue scraper.

* Incorporate a built-in toothpaste reservoir - A small spot on the handle could hold toothpaste, eliminating the need for a tube. You could just pump the toothpaste directly onto the bristles as needed.

* A toothbrush with different shaped heads for different brush needs - Flat, angled, tapered, etc. This would allow for effective cleaning in various mouth situations.

Again, these ideas are a starting point. You may need to do research, gather opinions, and even make prototypes to refine your idea. The important thing is to start by considering the object and where improvements could be made.

Imagine you are an emergency responder who has just been called to assist at the scene of an accident. Upon arrival, you see three victims: A, B, and C. Victim A has severe injuries and needs immediate surgery, victim B requires urgent medical attention but can wait a few minutes, and victim C is stable and requires minimal care. However, only two first responders are available, and each responder can only handle one victim at a time. How would you prioritize the care for the victims to ensure the greatest chance of survival?

In this triage situation, the goal is to prioritize care based on the severity of injuries and urgency of treatment to maximize survival rates. Here’s a step-by-step approach to prioritize the care:

- As soon as victim A is stabilized for surgery or the surgical team is ready, shift focus to victim B for urgent medical attention.

Solution :

To determine which job is more beneficial after 10 years, calculate the total earnings for each job over the decade.

**Job 1**: The first job is straightforward; it pays a flat $100,000 per year for 10 years.

\[ 100,000 \times 10 = \$1,000,000 \]

**Job 2**: The second job starts at $30,000 in the first year and increases by $5,000 each year. This is an arithmetic sequence where:

- The first term (a₁) is $30,000,
- The common difference (d) is $5,000,
- The number of terms (n) is 10.

\[ S_n = \frac{n}{2} \times (2a_1 + (n-1)d) \]

Plug in the values:

\[ S_{10} = 5 \times (60,000 + 45,000) \]

\[ S_{10} = \$525,000 \]

Cognitive Reflection Test

The Cognitive Reflection Test is a simple test designed to measure your ability to override your intuitive response and apply a more deliberative cognitive reasoning approach when needed. The test is made up of three questions. Here are the questions:

  1. A bat and ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
    A. 5 cents B. 10 cents C. 15 cents D. 20 cents

  2. If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?

  3. A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake. How long would it take the patch to cover half of the lake?

Here are the answers:

  1. If the ball costs 5 cents, and the bat costs $1 more, that means the bat would cost $1.05. The total cost would then be $1.05 + $0.05 = $1.10 which is correct. In other words, option A is the correct answer.
  2. If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, then it takes 1 machine 5 minutes to make 1 widget. Therefore, it would take 100 machines 5 minutes to make 100 widgets. So option D is the correct answer.
  3. If the lily patch doubles in size every day, then on the 47th day it would be ½ of the lake's size.

How'd you do? If you answered A, D, and C, you're not only a fast thinker but also someone who can override a quick but incorrect intuitive reaction. Not everyone gets all of these questions right. It's quite common for smart people to answer the first question incorrectly. This isn't because they don't have the intellectual capacity to answer correctly – it's just that their brains are wired to default to heuristics under time constraints. The trick is to take a moment and consciously override your initial response.

Remote Associates Test (RAT)

The Remote Associates Test (RAT) measures divergent thinking, creative thinking, and complex problem-solving abilities. You'll be given a group of three unrelated words. Your task is to find a fourth word that is semantically related to each word in the group. Here's an example:

Example Group: Candy, Sport, and Fast. Answer: Fasting

Here is another example: Book, February, and Leap. The answer is Year.

Here are a few more groups for you to try:

  1. Jelly, Burn, and Honey
  2. Axe, Fall, and Season
  3. Hair, Band, and Cream

Remember, the words in each group are completely arbitrary, so a straightforward or literal connection does not guarantee the correct answer. Keep an open mind and think laterally.

Answers are: 1) Smoke, 2) Break, 3) Soft

The good news is that no preparation is required for this test. Just give it everything you've got and see where you stand.

In summary, the CEB SHL Battery is designed to measure your cognitive and non-cognitive traits relevant to the workplace. The test components are:

  4. Make them waterproof, so they can be used on rainy days too
  5. Equip them with a GPS tracker so they can be tracked in case they're stolen or lost
  6. Make them more user friendly. This could involve making the controls more sensitive and making them easy to adjust for different users

  8. Make them solar powered so there's no need for battery replacement/charging
  9. Make them available with a range of customizable colors to allow the user to personalize their chair.
  10. Build them to include a storage compartment for personal items or luggage

These are just a few examples. You don't need to come up with this many ideas to score well. The important part is to make sure you're coming up with as many unique and sensible ideas as you can.

Cognitive Reflection Test

The Cognitive Reflection Test is a simple test designed to measure your ability to override your intuitive response and apply a more deliberative cognitive reasoning approach when needed. The test is made up of three questions. Here are the questions:

  1. A bat and ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
    A. 5 cents B. 10 cents C. 15 cents D. 20 cents

  2. If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?

  3. A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake. How long would it take the patch to cover half of the lake?

Here are the answers:

  1. If the ball costs 5 cents, and the bat costs $1 more, that means the bat would cost $1.05. The total cost would then be $1.05 + $0.05 = $1.10 which is correct. In other words, option A is the correct answer.
  2. If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, then it takes 1 machine 5 minutes to make 1 widget. Therefore, it would take 100 machines 5 minutes to make 100 widgets. So option D is the correct answer.
  3. If the lily patch doubles in size every day, then on the 47th day it would be ½ of the lake's size.

  3. Hair, Band, and Cream

To improve a waffle iron, one could create:
1. Multi-functional Waffle Iron: Incorporate various interchangeable plates or molds to transform the waffle iron into a panini press, egg-poaching skillet, or even a grilled cheese maker. This adds versatility to a single appliance, saving space and money for the user.

2. Indirect Warming Plate: Integrate a detachable warming plate underneath the grid to keep the cooked waffles warm while allowing the iron to prepare the next batch. This prevents over-crowding the freshly baked waffles and maintains optimal temperature.

3. Self-Cleaning System: Implement a non-stick, self-cleaning coating to reduce the hassle of scrubbing off baked-on batter from the iron's surface. This also extends the life and efficiency of the waffle iron.

4. Temperature Customization: Offer multiple heat settings that can be adjusted based on desired doneness, like a toaster setting, allowing for crispy, golden-brown waffles or softer, lighter ones depending on user preference.

5. Waffle Art Templates: Include customizable, interchangeable stencils or embossing plates that users can press into the batter before cooking. These templates could feature various designs, from simple patterns to elaborate pictures, creating artistic waffles.

6. Battery-Operated Model: Develop a portable waffle iron that operates on rechargeable batteries, ideal for camping, picnics, or outdoor events, eliminating the need for a power outlet and ensuring convenience.

7. Smart Waffle Maker App: Integrate a Bluetooth-enabled feature that connects the waffle iron to a smartphone app. Users can browse recipes, control cooking settings, set timers, and even receive notifications when their waffles are perfectly done.

8. Compact and Space-Saving Design: Design the waffle iron with a sleek, vertical profile that takes up minimal counter space, perfect for small kitchens or apartments. The design could include a foldable or collapsible handle for storage.

9. Eco-Friendly Options: Utilize sustainable, biodegradable materials in the construction of the waffle iron, such as using recycled metals or bio-based plastics, and ensuring energy efficiency.

10. LED Progress Indicator: Offer an LED light display that visually communicates the cooking progress and readiness of the waffles, ensuring uniform doneness and removing the guesswork.

11. Customizable Color Options: Provide a range of eye-catching color schemes and designs for personalization, allowing users to express their style while adding a pop of color to their kitchen decor.

12. Safety Features: Implement features such as automatic shut-off after a set time to prevent overheating or burning, child-lock settings, and heat-resistant handles to ensure safety during use.

13. Waffle Size Variety: Offer plates that accommodate waffle sizes ranging from standard to mini, catering to different serving portions and preferences.

14. Health-Conscious Options: Develop plates that allow for healthier variations, including provisions for low-sugar or gluten-free batters, enhancing the waffle iron's appeal to health-conscious consumers.

15. Integration With Home Automation Systems: Make the waffle iron compatible with popular smart home hubs, enabling voice activation and integration with routines or scenes, adding convenience and modernity to the cooking experience.

These ideas encapsulate a blend of functional enhancements, aesthetic appeals, safety considerations, and user convenience, aiming to elevate the humble waffle iron to a modern, versatile appliance cherished in any kitchen.

Creative Thinking Technique: Forced Connections
Creative Thinking Technique: Forced Connections | Source


This technique is a favorite of Edward de Bono, a creativity expert. Here's how forced connections work:

Step 1: Take two ideas that have no connection and force them together. The more unrelated the ideas appear, generally the more creative and innovative the end results will be.

Here are a few random pairs for you to try:

- Car and violin
- Shoe and snowball
- Chair and internet

Step 2: Now think about relationships between the two ideas. To help with this step, ask yourself these questions about each pair:

What is similar? (examples: Both car and violin have strings. Both shoe and snowball are thrown.)

What is different? (examples: Car has an engine but violin doesn't. Chair doesn't fly but internet can connect people thousands of miles apart.)

What could you combine? (examples: What if a violin string set was the same design as the gears in a car? What if shoes had little pockets of colored powder so when you walked, it left a snowball-like trail?)

What could you adapt? (examples: What would happen if the car frame was designed like a violin? What if shoes had built-in heaters to melt snow?)

What could you modify? (examples: Modify a violin into a portable karaoke machine. Modify snowballs into edible holiday treats.)

What can the ideas suggest? (examples: The violin could suggest the idea of using musical designs on vehicles. Shoes could lead you to consider self-heating, GPS tracking footwear.)

The objective is not to come up with practical ideas--at least not at first. Focus on exploring each connection and where it could lead. Sometimes the most impractical ideas can be turned into profitable innovations.



Creative Thinking Techniques: The Alternative Use

Creative Thinking Technique: The Alternative Use
Creative Thinking Technique: The Alternative Use | Source

The Alternative Use

When you hear the word "milk," what comes to mind? Most people will immediately think of drinking it, pouring it on cereal, or using it in cooking. But what else can it be used for?

The alternative use technique challenges you to identify different purposes for an object or to use it in a different way than you would usually think of. Here are some examples:

- Milk can be used to soothe sunburned skin.
- A plastic fork can double as a screwdriver to open packaging.
- An old sock can be fashioned into a puppet.
- A toothbrush can be used to apply wood stain.

This technique is about pushing past the obvious uses and asking "What else could it be good for?" Here are a couple more examples:

- What else could you do with nails (besides pounding them into wood)?
- How else can you use a shower curtain?

Don't limit yourself to thinking of uses within the same sphere. For instance, nails could be used as a gardening tool to mark plant rows or as a defensive weapon (don't do that). A shower curtain could serve as a makeshift painting tarp. The key is to think widely and not fear rejection of your ideas.



Creative Thinking Technique: Reinterpretation
Creative Thinking Technique: Reinterpretation | Source

Reinterpretation Technique

This is another of Edward de Bono's techniques. You take a subject and present it in a different way. The purpose is to gain new perspectives and insights. Here are some examples:

Reinterpret the word "deadline" - It's no longer a confining border but rather a motivational finish line.

Reinterpret a library - Picture it not as a room full of books but as a portal to unlimited education and adventure.

Reinterpret an assembly line - Instead of a rigid, repetitive process, it's a stream of creativity where each employee adds their unique twist to the end product.

What other subjects can you reinterpret? How about a "problem," "challenge," or "competition"?



Other Creative Thinking Techniques

SCAMPER: This is an acronym that stands for: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify/Magnify, Put to other use, Eliminate, and Reverse. As you can see, many of the ideas in this article fit into the SCAMPER categories. It's a process that systematically encourages you to think through different lenses.

Random Input: This involves selecting a random word or image and associating it with your subject to look at it in a new light.

Morphological Analysis: This is a way to break down a system and examine each component for possible changes, adaptations, or eliminations.

These techniques are just a few from the treasure trove available to help you harness your creativity and generate great ideas. Each one offers a new way to look at a subject and can be instrumental in solving problems or inventing innovations.

- Milk can be used to soothe sunburned skin.
- A plastic fork can double as a screwdriver to open packaging.
- An old sock can be fashioned into a puppet.
- A toothbrush can be used to apply wood stain.

This technique is about pushing past the obvious uses and asking "What else could it be good for?" Here are a couple more examples:

- What else could you do with nails (besides pounding them into wood)?
- How else can you use a shower curtain?

Don't limit yourself to thinking of uses within the same sphere. For instance, nails could be used as a gardening tool to mark plant rows or as a defensive weapon (don't do that). A shower curtain could serve as a makeshift painting tarp. The key is to think widely and not fear rejection of your ideas.

This is another of Edward de Bono's techniques. You take a subject and present it in a different way. The purpose is to gain new perspectives and insights. Here are some examples:

Reinterpret the word "deadline" - It's no longer a confining border but rather a motivational finish line.

Reinterpret a library - Picture it not as a room full of books but as a portal to unlimited education and adventure.

Reinterpret an assembly line - Instead of a rigid, repetitive process, it's a stream of creativity where each employee adds their unique twist to the end product.

What other subjects can you reinterpret? How about a "problem," "challenge," or "competition"?



Other Creative Thinking Techniques

SCAMPER: This is an acronym that stands for: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify/Magnify, Put to other use, Eliminate, and Reverse. As you can see, many of the ideas in this article fit into the SCAMPER categories. It's a process that systematically encourages you to think through different lenses.

Random Input: This involves selecting a random word or image and associating it with your subject to look at it in a new light.

Morphological Analysis: This is a way to break down a system and examine each component for possible changes, adaptations, or eliminations.

These techniques are just a few from the treasure trove available to help you harness your creativity and generate great ideas. Each one offers a new way to look at a subject and can be instrumental in solving problems or inventing innovations.

Now, we can explore the more advanced Creativity Techniques.

How to Improve Your Creativity: Creativity Techniques

A technique is a method of accomplishing something efficiently, and as such, it's a great way to break out of your mental ruts and access ideas that have been hidden away. There are scores of different techniques, and they all have fancy names, like Forced Association and Attribute Listing. But don't be intimidated... they're actually very simple to use.

Let's discuss a few, shall we?

1. Forced Association

Here's how Forced Association works:

Choose a random word. It can be random word from a book, magazine, or you can simply close your eyes and point to an object in the room.

Let's say the word is "cat."

Now, list all the words you associate with cat:

• Tail
• Furry
• Meow
• Small
• Hunt
• Purr
• Play
• Stubborn
• Whiskers
• Claws
• Soft
• Independent
• Sleep

Next, to these associations, add "How" or "What if." This will change the nature of the associations:

• How can I add a tail to this?
• What if it was furry?
• How can I make it purr?
• What if it hunts?
• ...

Notice how each question generates more ideas and takes your thinking in new directions. This technique is excellent for overcoming fixation on the obvious and encourages abstract thinking.

2. Attribute Listing

Here's how Attribute Listing works:

List the attributes of an object (qualities, aspects, properties, characteristics). If you pick something like a flower, you might list things like colors, scents, textures, size, shape, etc. Then ask, "How can I change this attribute?" or "What if I apply this attribute in a new context?"

For example, a flower can be:

• Red, blue, yellow, purple, etc.
• Sweet-smelling or stinky
• Soft and velvety or spiky
• Small or large
• Round or triangular
• Used in perfume, as flavoring in cooking, as home decoration, etc.

As you can see, attribute listing immediately expands your options and can lead to surprising and innovative ideas.

3. Random Entry

Random Entry is a great one for stimulating creativity and stretching your thinking. It's simple:

You start with a problem or challenge and write down a random word (or pick one from a magazine, book, etc.). Then, you explore the connections between the random word and your challenge. The crazier the word is, the more it will stimulate new thinking about the problem.

For example, if your challenge is, "How could we improve our employees' morale?" A random word is "elephant."

Ask yourself questions like:

• How are they alike?
• How can the word inspire a solution?
• What aspects of the word can be applied to the situation?

This might lead to thoughts about elephants being strong, having deep familial bonds, living in herds, being intelligent, etc. This can generate ideas like team-building events or perks that focus on social connection, implementing "memory" programs that note employees' work history and milestones, adding challenging but rewarding tasks to employees' routines, etc.

4. Challenge Assumptions

Here's how Challenge Assumptions works:

Start with your goal or challenge. Then, list the assumptions you and others are making about it. Ask yourself, "What if the opposite were true?" or "How can we negate this assumption?"

For example, if your goal is to decrease waiting time at a grocery store checkout:

• Assumption: There are not enough cashiers. What if there were always enough cashiers, no matter the volume of customers?
• Assumption: Customers have full carts. What if customers could only buy one item at a time?

Brainstorming against the assumptions will encourage fresh perspectives.

5. Harvesting

Harvesting is about gathering ideas from others so you can make new combinations from their ideas (this is known as intellectual cross-pollination). Here's how it works:

1. Gather ideas: Get input from a variety of diverse sources. These can be people from different fields and cultures or even ideas from books, movies, magazines, articles, etc.

2. Combine: Take these ideas and combine them in unique ways. For example, you could combine strategies from different historical battles, ideas from different authors, or elements from different cultures.

3. Iterate: Generate multiple iterations of your combined ideas.

Harvesting is invaluable for taking a "outsider-insider perspective." You're introducing outside ideas into an insider context and exploring the potential.

6. The SCAMPER Technique

The SCAMPER Technique is about manipulating or changing an object, idea or concept. It's an acronym that stands for:

• Substitute
• Combine
• Adapt
• Modify/Magnify
• Put to other uses
• Eliminate
• Reverse/Rearrange

Let's take the example of a guitar again:

• Substitute: Steel strings for nylon, Electric guitar for an acoustic, six strings for twelve...
• Combine: Two guitars into one, Guitar and turntable...
• Adapt: An underwater guitar, A motorcycle guitar...
• Magnify/Modify: Huge guitar strings for deep sounds, Guitar strings made from gold...
• Put to other uses: A sculpture instead of a musical instrument, A tool for cutting...
• Eliminate: Strings, the body, frets...
• Rearrange: Reverse the guitar so the resonating chamber faces backwards, Strings running from the bottom up...

The SCAMPER technique will systematically expand and evolve your ideas.

Try using some or all of the techniques above to stimulate your creativity. Remember, creativity is a skill; the more you practice, the better you'll get.

Want to improve your productivity? Here are 101 Ways to Improve Your Productivity.

Want to increase your effectiveness as a leader? Read our blog post on 15 Ways to Become a Better Leader Now.

If you love these techniques and want to learn more, I recommend two books:

• Thinkertoys: A Handbook of Creative Thinking Techniques - Michael Michalko

• Cracking Creativity: The Secrets of Creative Genius - Michael Michalko

The first book presents 52 creative-thinking techniques, and the second details the habits of creative geniuses. Both are great reads.

And speaking of reading, books are a fantastic resource for ideas. Read broadly and voraciously. Get your information from a diversity of subjects. The more ideas you're exposed to, the more connections you can make between seemingly unlike things. This is called associative thinking, and it's a superpower when it comes to creativity.

Let's wrap this up, shall we?

Applying It All

At this point, you have several creativity techniques at your disposal. Remember, don't force these; the goal is to stimulate your thinking, not stifle it. Instead, experiment and see which techniques resonate with you.

More importantly, make creativity a habit. Dedicate regular time to be creative—schedule "think sessions" the way you schedule other appointments. The more often you engage in these activities, the more nimble your brain becomes.

Lastly, share your ideas with others. They may be able to build on them, improve them, or inspire other innovations. Creativity thrives in communities.

Get out there, brainstorm, and innovate!

Now, we can explore the more advanced Creativity Techniques.

How to Improve Your Creativity: Creativity Techniques

A technique is a method of accomplishing something efficiently, and as such, it's a great way to break out of your mental ruts and access ideas that have been hidden away. There are scores of different techniques, and they all have fancy names, like Forced Association and Attribute Listing. But don't be intimidated... they're actually very simple to use.

Let's discuss a few, shall we?

1. Forced Association

Here's how Forced Association works:

Choose a random word. It can be random word from a book, magazine, or you can simply close your eyes and point to an object in the room.

Let's say the word is "cat."

Now, list all the words you associate with cat:

• Tail
• Furry
• Meow
• Small
• Hunt
• Purr
• Play
• Stubborn
• Whiskers
• Claws
• Soft
• Independent
• Sleep

Next, to these associations, add "How" or "What if." This will change the nature of the associations:

• How can I add a tail to this?
• What if it was furry?
• How can I make it purr?
• What if it hunts?
• ...

Notice how each question generates more ideas and takes your thinking in new directions. This technique is excellent for overcoming fixation on the obvious and encourages abstract thinking.

2. Attribute Listing

Here's how Attribute Listing works:

List the attributes of an object (qualities, aspects, properties, characteristics). If you pick something like a flower, you might list things like colors, scents, textures, size, shape, etc. Then ask, "How can I change this attribute?" or "What if I apply this attribute in a new context?"

For example, a flower can be:

• Red, blue, yellow, purple, etc.
• Sweet-smelling or stinky
• Soft and velvety or spiky
• Small or large
• Round or triangular
• Used in perfume, as flavoring in cooking, as home decoration, etc.

As you can see, attribute listing immediately expands your options and can lead to surprising and innovative ideas.

3. Random Entry

Random Entry is a great one for stimulating creativity and stretching your thinking. It's simple:

You start with a problem or challenge and write down a random word (or pick one from a magazine, book, etc.). Then, you explore the connections between the random word and your challenge. The crazier the word is, the more it will stimulate new thinking about the problem.

For example, if your challenge is, "How could we improve our employees' morale?" A random word is "elephant."

Ask yourself questions like:

• How are they alike?
• How can the word inspire a solution?
• What aspects of the word can be applied to the situation?

This might lead to thoughts about elephants being strong, having deep familial bonds, living in herds, being intelligent, etc. This can generate ideas like team-building events or perks that focus on social connection, implementing "memory" programs that note employees' work history and milestones, adding challenging but rewarding tasks to employees' routines, etc.

4. Challenge Assumptions

Here's how Challenge Assumptions works:

Start with your goal or challenge. Then, list the assumptions you and others are making about it. Ask yourself, "What if the opposite were true?" or "How can we negate this assumption?"

For example, if your goal is to decrease waiting time at a grocery store checkout:

• Assumption: There are not enough cashiers. What if there were always enough cashiers, no matter the volume of customers?
• Assumption: Customers have full carts. What if customers could only buy one item at a time?

Brainstorming against the assumptions will encourage fresh perspectives.

5. Harvesting

Harvesting is about gathering ideas from others so you can make new combinations from their ideas (this is known as intellectual cross-pollination). Here's how it works:

1. Gather ideas: Get input from a variety of diverse sources. These can be people from different fields and cultures or even ideas from books, movies, magazines, articles, etc.

2. Combine: Take these ideas and combine them in unique ways. For example, you could combine strategies from different historical battles, ideas from different authors, or elements from different cultures.

3. Iterate: Generate multiple iterations of your combined ideas.

Harvesting is invaluable for taking a "outsider-insider perspective." You're introducing outside ideas into an insider context and exploring the potential.

6. The SCAMPER Technique

The SCAMPER Technique is about manipulating or changing an object, idea or concept. It's an acronym that stands for:

• Substitute
• Combine
• Adapt
• Modify/Magnify
• Put to other uses
• Eliminate
• Reverse/Rearrange

Let's take the example of a guitar again:

• Substitute: Steel strings for nylon, Electric guitar for an acoustic, six strings for twelve...
• Combine: Two guitars into one, Guitar and turntable...
• Adapt: An underwater guitar, A motorcycle guitar...
• Magnify/Modify: Huge guitar strings for deep sounds, Guitar strings made from gold...
• Put to other uses: A sculpture instead of a musical instrument, A tool for cutting...
• Eliminate: Strings, the body, frets...
• Rearrange: Reverse the guitar so the resonating chamber faces backwards, Strings running from the bottom up...

The SCAMPER technique will systematically expand and evolve your ideas.

Try using some or all of the techniques above to stimulate your creativity. Remember, creativity is a skill; the more you practice, the better you'll get.

The first book presents 52 creative-thinking techniques, and the second details the habits of creative geniuses. Both are great reads.

And speaking of reading, books are a fantastic resource for ideas. Read broadly and voraciously. Get your information from a diversity of subjects. The more ideas you're exposed to, the more connections you can make between seemingly unlike things. This is called associative thinking, and it's a superpower when it comes to creativity.

Applying It All

At this point, you have several creativity techniques at your disposal. Remember, don't force these; the goal is to stimulate your thinking, not stifle it. Instead, experiment and see which techniques resonate with you.

More importantly, make creativity a habit. Dedicate regular time to be creative—schedule "think sessions" the way you schedule other appointments. The more often you engage in these activities, the more nimble your brain becomes.

Lastly, share your ideas with others. They may be able to build on them, improve them, or inspire other innovations. Creativity thrives in communities.

Solar panels and wind turbines can be seen more frequently in urban landscapes. Rooftop gardens are becoming popular as they help mitigate the heat island effect and provide green spaces.

As cities become more aware of the urgent need for sustainable practices, you might even see policies mandating green roofs and facades. This is where rooftops and building exteriors are covered in vegetation. They help absorb CO2, retain rainwater, and reduce energy consumption.

Sustainable farming practices and urban agriculture are gaining traction. Vertical farms, for example, grow crops in vertically stacked layers, significantly reducing the need for land and water. This could transform how cities obtain food, reduce CO2 emissions from transportation, and limit food waste.

1. Find someone willing to make the trip overseas. 2. Write a letter explaining the situation. 3. Find a courier service to bring the letter to the recipient. 4. Wait for the courier to do his/her job.


Let's suppose you're writing the letter in English and your correspondent understands the language. For that letter to be effective, you need to consider your choice of words and sentence structure carefully.

The sentences in English can take two basic forms: simple or compound. In the simple sentence, one complete thought is expressed, and it starts with a capital letter and ends with a period, question mark or exclamation point.

On the other hand, compound sentences consist of two or more simple sentences joined by coordination or subordination conjunctions.

Coordinating conjunctions are used to connect the equal elements (words, phrases or clauses) in a sentence. They include: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (the acronym is FANBOYS).

Examples of compound sentences:

  • She read the book and she took notes. (joining with "and")

  • He is not going to the meeting, nor is he answering any phone calls. (joining with "nor")

  • I like to play soccer, but I don't enjoy watching it. (joining with "but")

  • Should we order pizza or Chinese take-out for dinner? (joining with "or")

  • She wanted to go to the concert, yet she decided to stay home with her kids. (joining with "yet")

  • He didn't study for the test, so he failed. (joining with "so")

On the other hand, subordinating conjunctions are used at the beginning of a dependent (subordinate) clause - that part of a sentence that cannot stand alone as a separate sentence.

Here is a list of common subordinating conjunctions: after, although, as, as if, as long as, as though, because, before, even if, even though, if, in order that, since, so that, though, unless, until, when, whenever, where, where clause, whereas, wherever, while.

Examples of sentences beginning with subordinating conjunctions:

  • After finishing her work, she went for a walk.

  • Although I was tired, I kept studying.

  • I'll only go to the party if you come too.

  • Because she studied hard, she got an A on the test.

  • Before we leave, we should do the shopping.

  • If you need help, call me.

  • In order that the flowers last longer, I put them in the refrigerator.

Now, let's try to write the letter:

Dear [Recipient's name],

Since electronic communication is currently not an option, I am writing this letter in the hope that it reaches you safely. I trust you are doing well, and I wanted to inform you of the current situation in my life.

Although I have been experiencing a series of challenges lately, I remain resilient and positive. Despite the difficulties, I am doing my best to face each day courageously. As you know, I am someone who believes in the power of perseverance.

Because we have been such good friends for years, I thought you would be the first person I'd contact. Having said that, I am aware of how difficult it would be to send this letter overseas, so I have attached a list of local couriers who can handle the job. Please choose the one that fits your budget and schedule.

While I understand that this method of communication is far from ideal, I trust it's effective. Therefore, I sincerely hope this letter reaches you promptly and that we can maintain our friendship through this unconventional means.

I look forward to hearing from you soon, and please take care.

Best regards,

[Your name]

Question: If all electronic communication were to suddenly cease, how would you contact someone in another country? Let's think step by step.
Answer:  1. Find someone willing to make the trip overseas. 2. Write a letter explaining the situation. 3. Find a courier service to bring the letter to the recipient. 4. Wait for the courier to do his/her job.


Let's suppose you're writing the letter in English and your correspondent understands the language. For that letter to be effective, you need to consider your choice of words and sentence structure carefully.

The sentences in English can take two basic forms: simple or compound. In the simple sentence, one complete thought is expressed, and it starts with a capital letter and ends with a period, question mark or exclamation point.

On the other hand, compound sentences consist of two or more simple sentences joined by coordination or subordination conjunctions.

Coordinating conjunctions are used to connect the equal elements (words, phrases or clauses) in a sentence. They include: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (the acronym is FANBOYS).

Examples of compound sentences:

  • She read the book and she took notes. (joining with "and")

  • He is not going to the meeting, nor is he answering any phone calls. (joining with "nor")

  • I like to play soccer, but I don't enjoy watching it. (joining with "but")

  • Should we order pizza or Chinese take-out for dinner? (joining with "or")

  • She wanted to go to the concert, yet she decided to stay home with her kids. (joining with "yet")

  • He didn't study for the test, so he failed. (joining with "so")

On the other hand, subordinating conjunctions are used at the beginning of a dependent (subordinate) clause - that part of a sentence that cannot stand alone as a separate sentence.

Here is a list of common subordinating conjunctions: after, although, as, as if, as long as, as though, because, before, even if, even though, if, in order that, since, so that, though, unless, until, when, whenever, where, where clause, whereas, wherever, while.

Examples of sentences beginning with subordinating conjunctions:

  • After finishing her work, she went for a walk.

  • Although I was tired, I kept studying.

  • I'll only go to the party if you come too.

  • Because she studied hard, she got an A on the test.

  • Before we leave, we should do the shopping.

  • If you need help, call me.

  • In order that the flowers last longer, I put them in the refrigerator.
